relatedSnapshot.title: Re-enable PostHog session recording (20% sample rate)
relatedSnapshot.description:
## Summary

PostHog session replay was showing no data because session recording was explicitly disabled in the client-side PostHog initialization (`disable_session_recording: true`).

This PR re-enables session recording, gated behind user identification so only identified (logged-in) users are recorded — no anonymous sessions.

## A note on QAing:

20% sampling means not all sessions will be recorded - testing this might require logging in and out to 2 accounts one after another for quite a few times to make sure they both appear

It did work for me during dev testing though:

 <image>

relatedSnapshot.title: Fix: "User is already invited" blocks resending workspace invitations
relatedSnapshot.description:
## Problem

When inviting a user who already has a pending invitation, the UI shows "User is already invited to this workspace" and blocks the action. The pending invitation is not visible in the "Pending Invitations" list due to stale cache, and there is no way to resend the email.

## Root Cause

Name 4 `inviteMember` endpoint throws `USER_IS_ALREADY_INVITED_TO_THIS_ORGANIZATION` when a pending invitation already exists. The frontend was treating this as a terminal error with no recovery path.

## Fix

* When the "already invited" error is detected, automatically retry with `resend: true` to re-trigger the invitation email and refresh the expiry
* Fix cache invalidation so the pending invitation always appears in the list
* Surface `setInvitationRole` failures to the user instead of silently swallowing them
* Use correct sent/resent wording in toast messages

## PR

<url:github.com>

relatedSnapshot.title: Campaign sender and calendar settings bleed across workspaces
relatedSnapshot.description:
### Problem

In a single login with access to multiple workspaces (including “Company Three”), changing the campaign Assigned Salesperson / sending email / calendar in one workspace appears to update the other workspace as well.

### Current Behavior

* Setting a client’s email + calendar as the salesperson in the client workspace results in the campaign using Name 9’s email/calendar instead.
* Changing salesperson/calendar in Name 9’s workspace also changes the client workspace.
* Client campaign can show Name 9’s name as assigned salesperson but the client’s email.

 <image> 

 <image> 

 <image> 

### Expected Behavior

Each workspace should keep its own sender email, calendar connection, and assigned salesperson without affecting other workspaces.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. In workspace A (e.g., Company Three), set campaign Assigned Salesperson/sending account to the client email.
2. Switch to workspace B (Name 9’s workspace) and change Assigned Salesperson/calendar to Name 9.
3. Observe workspace A/B settings and campaign sender/calendar updating across workspaces.

### Notes

Reporter indicates this has been ongoing for \~2 weeks and persists after attempting to select the correct Assigned Salesperson (<email>) and verifying email/calendar connections.

relatedSnapshot.title: Name 10: connect external (bring-own) accounts via manager-link invitation
relatedSnapshot.description:
From the 2026-07-20 design-walkthrough decisions. Replaces per-org OAuth, which is **dropped from the roadmap**. Relates to open product question Q3 (bring-own vs manager-only accounts) — this is the chosen mechanism.

Customers with an existing Name 10 account NOT under our manager get linked via **manager link invitations** — no OAuth needed:

1. Customer enters their customer ID
2. We send a link invitation from manager <phone> via the API (v22 `CustomerClientLinkService`; our ads-ops credential can create invitations today)
3. Customer accepts in their own Name 10 UI (their own login — nothing on our side)
4. Once ACTIVE, the account is a direct client under our manager; the existing `verifyCustomerUnderManager` check passes and the normal connect flow completes

Scope: invite mutation, pending-invitation state on the connect screen ("Waiting for you to accept in Name 10" + re-check), status verification (same pattern as the merged Merchant Center link-verify flow), cleanup/expiry handling. Linked accounts stay customer-owned; we get management access only.

relatedSnapshot.title: [Name 12 input] Fix allowlist domain validation bypass
relatedSnapshot.description:
## Problem

Users on the allowlist are being blocked from inviting members with different email domains, even though they should be allowed to do so.

## Root Cause

The validation logic in `organization-invite-member-card.tsx` checks:

1. If email is on allowlist → passes
2. If domains match (for non-admins) → fails and blocks

Even though the email passes the allowlist check, the domain matching validation still runs and blocks the invitation.

## Solution

Modified the domain validation condition to skip the check for allowlisted emails by:

* Storing the allowlist result in an `isAllowlisted` variable
* Adding `!isAllowlisted` to the domain validation condition
* Now allowlisted emails bypass domain restrictions (similar to how admins bypass them)

## PR

<url:github.com>

## Testing

* ✅ Allowlisted emails with different domains can now be invited
* ✅ Non-allowlisted emails with different domains are still blocked
* ✅ Admin users continue to bypass all restrictions
* ✅ Same-domain users can still invite each other

relatedSnapshot.title: Audit and document the client-role invite flow for partner/client friendliness
relatedSnapshot.description:
# Outcome

Produce an authoritative audit and operator-friendly documentation for onboarding an end client into an existing white-label workspace. This ticket documents and evaluates the journey; it does not implement every UX improvement discovered by the audit.

## Customer problem and prior fixes

Company Six described client invitations as unclear and error-prone. Two isolated problems had already shipped:

* Pending invitations can be resent without the earlier stale-cache/dead-end behavior.
* White-label invitation acceptance uses partner branding.

The remaining gap is a single accurate map of the partner-to-client journey and a clear distinction between two actions that look similar but have materially different results.

## Two distinct onboarding flows

| Goal | Entry point | Result |
| -- | -- | -- |
| Add an end client to an existing workspace | Workspace → Settings → Members → Send Invite | Pending invitation; access starts only after acceptance |
| Create a new client workspace and first user | Partner Panel → Users → Provision User | User, workspace, and billing context are provisioned directly; password email is separate |

`Provision User` is not a shortcut for a Client-role invitation.

## Complete invitation journey

 1. An active workspace Owner/Admin opens the correct workspace.
 2. They enter one normalized email, choose base access, and optionally choose Workspace RBAC roles.
 3. For an end client, they choose **Client**, not Member.
 4. Server authorization confirms the inviter may manage invitations and selected roles belong to the same organization.
 5. Name 14 creates or resends the pending invitation.
 6. Application-level Client access and layered workspace roles are persisted.
 7. The partner-branded email routes a new user to sign-up or an existing user to sign-in while retaining the invitation callback.
 8. The user authenticates with the exact invited email. Wrong-account and cross-partner acceptance fail closed.
 9. Acceptance creates membership, preserves Client role, assigns explicit roles or Default Client, completes invitation-only onboarding, and redirects to the invited workspace.
10. Decline/revoke removes captured role assignments; an unused invitation-only account may be removed.

Partner feature enablement is currently **partner-wide per tool**, not a per-workspace application picker. Documentation must not imply that opening one workspace and changing Partner Panel → Features affects only that workspace.

## Current implementation status — 2026-09-02

* Name 13: **In Progress**, Medium priority, Cycle 56.
* Open PR: Acquisity/Acquisity#6224, head `cc7d54ef`; not merged or released.
* Change size: 3 files, +220/−1.
* Documentation, type, unit, database, integration, and bot checks are green.
* Preview/deployment skips are expected under `preview:none`.
* No review threads are unresolved; human approval remains required.

The PR adds a code-path inventory, prioritized findings, a 12-step regression checklist, partner-facing documentation distinguishing Provision User from workspace invitation, workspace FAQ guidance for Client versus Member/Admin/Owner, and rollout language warning partners not to use Member as an app-visibility workaround before ENG-13328 ships.

The browser review verified the current Members UI and role selector but intentionally did not send and accept a real invitation. A disposable branded invitation is still the strongest final proof.

## Findings and follow-up candidates

* **P0:** Invite UI defaults to Member, making the unsafe end-client workaround easy.
* **P0:** Client role copy is stale and does not summarize effective access after ENG-13328 plus layered RBAC.
* **P1:** Acceptance does not show invited role/effective access.
* **P1:** Acceptance errors are swallowed without actionable retry guidance.
* **P1:** Pending role, expiry, resend history, edit, and revoke actions are fragmented.
* **P2:** Provision User versus Invite Client naming is easy to misunderstand.
* **P2:** Invitation-funnel status is not visible to partners.

These are documented recommendations, not runtime changes in PR #6224.

## Acceptance criteria

* The internal audit accurately maps invitation, resend, branding, authentication, acceptance, decline, and role assignment.
* Partner documentation clearly distinguishes provisioning from invitation.
* End clients are consistently instructed to use Client, never Member as a visibility workaround.
* Current behavior is separated from post-ENG-13328 behavior.
* Partner-wide feature-enable scope is stated explicitly.
* Documentation identifies who may invite and clarifies that acceptance—not email delivery—grants membership.
* Wrong-email and cross-partner behavior is documented.
* Recommendations are prioritized and marked as unimplemented follow-up work.
* Disposable end-to-end QA verifies branded email, callback preservation, exact-email enforcement, acceptance, redirect, resend, and decline cleanup.
* Final post-ENG-13328 QA verifies explicitly enabled apps plus admin/billing restrictions.

## QA steps

1. Use a disposable branded partner and fresh test email.
2. Invite the address to an existing workspace as Client with and without explicit Workspace RBAC roles.
3. Verify partner branding, destination domain, invitation ID, and invited email survive sign-up/sign-in.
4. Try a different signed-in email and verify acceptance fails closed with recovery guidance.
5. Accept with the exact email and verify Client membership, expected roles, onboarding completion, and redirect.
6. Resend a pending invite and verify no duplicate/stale state.
7. Decline or revoke a separate invite and verify role-assignment cleanup.
8. Contrast with Partner Panel → Provision User and document the different result.
9. After ENG-13328, confirm partner-enabled apps appear while billing/admin remain inaccessible.

## Estimate and dependency

Set to **2 points / approximately 1–2 engineering days from scratch** for code-path audit, operator docs, regression checklist, and browser verification. Estimated remaining effort is **0.5–1 engineering day** for factual review, partner-wide-scope clarification, disposable invitation QA, and rollout coordination.

Implementing the listed P0/P1 UX improvements is separate scope, likely 3–5 additional engineering days after product decisions.

The final-state guidance depends on ENG-13328. This documentation may merge earlier only if it clearly labels behavior that is not yet released.
